comparator.route: Sustainable City and Safe City themes; thesis graduation track; Urban Arts, Culture and Society thesis pathway
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 catalogue and regulations support 60 EC in each year. Year two requires one thematic and one methods elective per semester. Humanities and Urbanism is first-listed in semester one and advised for the selected thesis track. Linear Models in semester two requires Inferential Statistics, so Spatial Analysis and Modelling is the eligible second-semester choice on this pathway. The third year includes a literature seminar, a 25 EC graduation pathway and 30 EC of open study.

alternatives.concept: This programme studies climate-resilient cities through climate and Earth science, biodiversity, flood management, circular materials and renewable energy. GIS and spatial planning connect environmental evidence to decisions about land, infrastructure and risk. Economics, governance and an applied sustainability project provide further perspectives on those decisions.

comparatorRouteSelection.route: Sustainable City and Safe City themes; thesis graduation track; Urban Arts, Culture and Society thesis pathway
comparatorRouteSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic Urban Studies bachelor. The official curriculum requires two of four themes and offers a thesis or Urban Environmental Science graduation route. No route is established as uniquely primary. Sustainable City and Safe City are the first two themes on the current public programme page; the ordinary thesis route matches the programme page's standard description of completion through an interdisciplinary thesis; and the Urban Arts, Culture and Society options appear first within that route. These neutral order choices do not use UCR fit.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Three evidence-backed UCR programmes are feasible and pairwise distinct by at least four courses: a broad cities, society and governance route; a sustainable and climate-resilient cities route; and a safe and healthy urban communities route. Cultural diversity and the multicultural-city direction are substantively covered by the broad route rather than manufactured as a fourth programme.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both examine institutions and public authority; UCR is comparative politics rather than a dedicated urban-governance course.
Both address law, justice and social responses to harm; Leiden focuses specifically on crime and criminalisation in the city.
Criminal law and justice provide a direct institutional lens on the Safe City theme, without reproducing its full urban scope.
Leiden's programme-specific Urban Studies foundation has no single UCR course counterpart.
The programme-specific Reading the City component has no sufficiently direct UCR counterpart.
No single UCR course covers the history and practice of urban planning across multiple cities.
Both study social groups, inequality and community structure; Leiden applies these specifically to urban cultural diversity.
Both examine social determinants of behaviour; Leiden embeds them in Urban Studies.
Both study how communication constructs public meaning, while Leiden focuses on representations of the city.
Both analyse language, power and identity; Leiden applies them to multicultural and multilingual cities.
Both engage advanced social theory and civil society; Leiden's seminar is explicitly centred on urban theory and philosophy.
Both develop qualitative research design and interpretation.
Both address population health and wellbeing; Leiden places the topic specifically in cities.
Both examine climate change, impacts and adaptation; Leiden integrates these within the Sustainable City theme.
Both address biodiversity and governance; Leiden's elective is specifically about biodiversity in cities.
Both use spatial analysis and modelling; UCR emphasises GIS and Earth-observation data.
Both develop GIS and spatial analysis through applied projects. Leiden focuses on spatial questions in cities.
Both examine material flows, reuse and environmental impacts; UCR focuses on recovery and remediation.
Both develop academic writing, presentation and collaborative skills; UCR also includes personal and professional development.
Both introduce research design and quantitative methods.
The urban-humanities methodology elective has no sufficiently direct UCR course counterpart.
The selected programme-specific thesis seminar has no ordinary UCR course counterpart.
The selected programme-specific Urban Studies research lab has no ordinary UCR course counterpart.
Leiden's compulsory 10-EC Urban Studies thesis remains distinct from ordinary UCR courses and from UCR's optional research opportunity.
The genuine 30-EC elective, minor, internship or study-abroad space remains open and is not treated as fixed urban content.

notes.text: Leiden offers an integrated Urban Studies sequence with city-specific foundations, thematic lectures, electives, methods, a research lab and a compulsory thesis. UCR can construct three coherent urban-focused programmes from governance, sociology, law, health, sustainability, environmental science and research methods, but it does not reproduce the same dedicated Urban Studies core; shared rows indicate substantive overlap rather than course equivalence.

audience.programmeDescription: Leiden’s English-taught Urban Studies degree combines social science, humanities and environmental research to study how cities work and change. Students investigate urban sustainability, safety, health and diversity through thematic courses, field and research methods, and a graduation project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The three UCR options explore cities through governance and society, climate resilience and spatial planning, or community safety and health. They share some methods and subject matter with Leiden. Leiden provides a dedicated urban studies core, city-specific research training and a required graduation pathway.
